subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The Deadly City-to-City Races
description: One-minute skill: The Deadly City-to-City Races.

hook.text: After Paris-Rouen, races between cities became wildly popular—and incredibly dangerous.

buildup.text: Cars raced through towns on open roads shared with pedestrians, horses, and cyclists.

discovery.text: The 1903 Paris-Madrid race killed so many people that the French government stopped it midway.

twist.text: Drivers, mechanics, and spectators died because nobody thought speed on public roads needed limits.

climax.text: The disaster ended city-to-city racing and forced organizers to build dedicated closed circuits.

punchline.text: The deadliest race ever created the need for racetracks.

quiz.question: What happened during the 1903 Paris-Madrid race?
options: It was cancelled due to rain
It was stopped midway due to fatal crashes
The cars were too slow to finish

details.summary: Early automobile races between European cities in the 1890s and 1900s were run on public roads with no safety measures, leading to fatal crashes that prompted authorities to ban open-road racing.
details.whyItMatters: The deadly Paris-Madrid race of 1903, which killed multiple drivers and spectators, forced governments to create purpose-built circuits and safety regulations that shaped modern motorsport.
takeaways: Paris-Bordeaux in 1895 was one of the first city-to-city races
The 1903 Paris-Madrid race was stopped after multiple fatalities
Deaths prompted the creation of closed circuits like Brooklands

faq.question: How many people died in the 1903 Paris-Madrid race?
faq.answer: At least eight people died, including drivers, mechanics, and spectators. The French government stopped the race in Bordeaux, and surviving cars were towed back to Paris. It was called the Race of Death.

faq.question: Did the ban on open-road racing apply everywhere?
faq.answer: Most of Western Europe banned open-road racing. Italy's Mille Miglia continued on public roads until a 1957 crash killed 12, and the Targa Florio in Sicily ran until 1977 before safety concerns ended it.
